I. 
INTRODUCTION 
 
In this Order, subject to the modifications discussed below, the Vermont Public Utility 
Commission (“Commission”) approves a new alternative regulation plan (the “Plan”) for 
Vermont Gas Systems, Inc. (“VGS”), pursuant to 30 V.S.A. § 218d.  As approved, the Plan will 
govern adjustments to the gas and non-gas components of VGS’s rates for its firm customers for 
a three-year term with an option for VGS to seek a one-year extension.  The Plan includes 
various mechanisms that will adjust VGS’s base rates and natural gas costs based on specified 
inflation indices, fluctuations in wholesale natural gas costs, and a fixed plan for VGS’s capital 
expenditures.  The Plan also includes provisions that will allow VGS to pursue new innovative 
services and increase its use of alternative fuels to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and 
otherwise pursue Vermont’s broader energy policies and goals.  
 
As discussed in more detail below, we conclude that the Plan meets the statutory criteria 
set out in 30 V.S.A. § 218d—including promoting innovation, the provision of safe and reliable 
service, and setting just and reasonable rates.

II. 
PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
 
On November 30, 2022, VGS filed a petition seeking approval of a new alternative 
regulation plan.  The petition was supported by a draft of the proposed Plan and the prefiled 
direct testimony and exhibits of Andrea McNeil (“McNeil pf.”) and Gregory Morse (“Morse 
pf.”). 
 
On December 16, 2022, the Commission held a scheduling conference for this case, 
which was attended by representatives of the Vermont Department of Public Service 
(“Department”) and VGS. 
 
On January 30, 2023, the Commission conducted a workshop with representatives from 
VGS and the Department. 
 
On February 9, 2023, the Commission issued information requests to VGS. 
 
On March 10, 2023, VGS filed responses to the Commission’s information requests.  
VGS’s responses were supported by the prefiled supplemental testimony and exhibits of Andrea 
McNeil (“McNeil pf. supp.”) and Gregory Morse (“Morse pf. supp.”) and a revised draft of the 
proposed Plan. 
 
On April 7, 2023, the Department filed the prefiled direct testimony and exhibits of Sean 
Foley (“Foley pf.”) and Adam Jacobs (“Jacobs pf.”). 
 
On April 20, 2023, the Commission issued information requests to the Department. 
 
On May 5, 2023, the Department filed responses to the Commission’s information 
requests.  The Department’s responses were supported by the prefiled supplemental testimony of 
Sean Foley (“Foley pf. supp.”) and Adam Jacobs (“Jacobs pf. supp.”). 
 
On May 19, 2023, VGS filed the prefiled rebuttal testimony and exhibits of Andrea 
McNeil (“McNeil pf. reb.”) and Gregory Morse (“Morse pf. reb.”). 
 
On June 9, 2023, the Department filed the prefiled rebuttal testimony of Adam Jacobs 
(“Jacobs pf. reb.”). 
 
On June 16, 2023, Pike Porter, a member of the public, filed comments with the 
Commission raising substantive concerns with VGS’s proposed Plan and requesting that 
Commissioner Allen recuse himself from this case.  The Commission also received one other 
comment from another member of the public on June 16, 2023.

On June 19, 2023, the Commission held an evidentiary hearing for this case.  At the 
outset of the evidentiary hearing, before taking any evidence, Chair Roisman and Commissioner 
Cheney addressed Mr. Porter’s public comment and request that Commissioner Allen be recused 
from this case.  The Commissioners issued an oral ruling that Commissioner Allen is not 
required to recuse himself from this case.  During the evidentiary hearing, the Commission also 
admitted into the evidentiary record Exhibit Commission-1, which includes a list of all prefiled 
testimony and exhibits that were admitted into the evidentiary record.  The evidentiary hearing 
was attended by VGS, the Department, and several members of the public. 
 
On June 30, 2023, VGS and the Department filed legal briefs. 
 
On July 12, 2023, VGS and the Department filed reply briefs. 
 
  
III. 
PUBLIC COMMENTS 
 
Over the course of this proceeding, the Commission received four written comments 
from members of the public, including three comments from Mr. Porter and a comment from one 
other member of the public.  Both commenters wrote in opposition to VGS’s proposed Plan.  
They raised concerns about the environmental impacts of VGS’s business practices.  They also 
addressed portions of the proposed Plan that would allow VGS to increase its supply of 
alternative fuel sources and assist municipalities in pursuing district heat projects.  In particular, 
they questioned whether emissions reductions can be achieved through the use of renewable 
natural gas (“RNG”) and biomass as alternative fuel sources for natural gas.  The commenters 
stated that the Plan, if approved, will lead to increased greenhouse gas emissions. 
 
We agree with the commenters that the environmental impacts of VGS’s business 
practices, particularly greenhouse gas emissions, are an important consideration for our review of 
the proposed Plan.  Indeed, as we have discussed in other recent cases, VGS will need to 
substantially transform its overall business practices to adapt to Vermont’s broader energy 
policies and environmental objectives.1  We note that the enactment of the Affordable Heat Act, 
which was ratified by the Vermont Legislature during the pendency of this case, highlights the 
primacy of the carbon-reduction considerations that are likely to factor into our regulatory 
 
1 See, e.g., Petition of Vermont Gas Systems, Inc., pursuant to 30 V.S.A. § 248(i), for approval of an out-of-state 
renewable gas purchase contract with a term exceeding 5 years, Case 22-2230-PET, Order of 11/08/11.

Case No. 22-5085-PET 
 
Page 5 
 
 
review of VGS’s business practices for the foreseeable future.2  However, 30 V.S.A. § 218d 
directs that our review of VGS’s proposed Plan, especially with respect to VGS’s rates, remain 
tethered to traditional regulatory and ratemaking standards.3  Thus, in reviewing VGS’s proposed 
Plan, we seek to strike an appropriate balance between providing VGS with flexibility to pursue 
and experiment with new services directed at mitigating its greenhouse gas impacts and adhering 
to traditional ratemaking standards to ensure adequate and meaningful protections for VGS’s 
ratepayers—in particular those who remain reliant on VGS for a critical utility service.  As 
discussed below, we conclude that VGS’s proposed Plan, subject to the revisions that we detail 
in this Order, strikes this balance and satisfies the applicable criteria under Section 218d.  
However, we also recognize that our regulatory policy will continue to evolve to ensure that 
VGS adheres to the environmental and emission mandates codified in Vermont law as those 
mandates take effect in the future. 
 
We appreciate the comments that we received in this case, which were thoughtful and 
raised issues that are germane to our review of VGS’s proposed Plan.  They informed our review 
of this case and will aid in framing related issues in future proceedings involving VGS.  We also 
note that approval of the Plan does not constitute approval of any specific contracts or projects 
involving alternative fuel sources.  The Plan includes various mechanisms that will ensure our 
ongoing regulatory oversight over VGS’s spending on new initiatives as they arise over the term 
of the Plan. 
IV. 
LEGAL STANDARD 
The Commission is authorized by 30 V.S.A. § 218d to approve alternative regulation 
plans for electric and natural gas companies.  The Commission, on its own motion or on the 
motion of the Department or a company operating under an alternative regulation plan, may 
investigate any alternative regulation plan that is in effect and, following notice and an 
 
2 Public Act No. 18 (2023 Vt., Bien. Sess.). 
3 See 30 V.S.A. § 218d(1)-(3) (“[T]he Commission shall find that the proposed form of alternative regulation 
will: (1) establish a system of regulation in which such companies have clear incentives to provide least cost energy 
service to their customers; (2) provide just and reasonable rates for service to all classes of customers; and (3) 
deliver safe and reliable service . . . .”).

Case No. 22-5085-PET 
 
Page 6 
 
 
opportunity for hearing, may terminate or modify the alternative regulation plan upon a finding 
of good cause.4 
In order to rule favorably on requests to establish or amend an alternative regulation plan, 
we must find that the proposed form of alternative regulation will: 
(1) establish a system of regulation in which . . . companies have clear incentives 
to provide least-cost energy service to their customers;  
(2) provide just and reasonable rates for service to all classes of customers; 
(3) deliver safe and reliable service; 
(4) offer incentives for innovations and improved performance that advance state 
energy policy such as increasing reliance on Vermont-based renewable energy 
and decreasing the extent to which the financial success of distribution 
utilities between rate cases is linked to increased sales to end use customers 
and may be threatened by decreases in those sales; 
(5) promote improved quality of service, reliability, and service choices; 
(6) encourage innovation in the provision of service; 
(7) establish a reasonably balanced system of risks and rewards that encourages 
the company to operate as efficiently as possible using sound management 
practices; and 
(8) provide a reasonable opportunity, under sound and economical management, 
to earn a fair rate of return, provided such opportunity must be consistent with 
flexible design of alternative regulation and with the inclusion of effective 
financial incentives in such alternatives.5 
In the case of an investor-owned company such as VGS, the Commission will approve an 
alternative regulation plan only if we find that the plan “will not have an adverse impact on 
[VGS’s] eligibility for rate-regulated accounting in accordance with generally accepted 
accounting standards if applicable; and reasonably preserve the availability of equity and debt 
capital resources to the company on favorable terms and conditions.”6 
Finally, alternative regulation may include changes or alternatives to traditional 
ratemaking procedures, standards, and mechanisms, as long as the Commission finds that 
alternative regulation will promote the public good and will support the required findings in 30 
V.S.A. § 218d(a).7

V. 
FINDINGS 
A. 
Summary of the Plan as Proposed 
Structure and Term of the Plan 
1. The Plan will become effective on October 1, 2023, and be implemented with bills 
rendered on or after November 1, 2023.  The Plan includes an initial term of three years and will 
expire on September 30, 2026.  VGS proposes that the Plan include an option that would allow 
VGS to seek Commission approval for a two-year extension of the Plan.  McNeil pf. at 9; exh. 
VGS-ALM-4 at 1. 
2. The stated goals of the Plan are to regulate VGS’s rates and to fulfill the objectives of 
30 V.S.A. § 218d(a), including providing smooth and transparent rates for customers, supporting 
VGS’s provision of safe and reliable service, decreasing the link between VGS’s financial 
outcomes and its retail sales, and encouraging innovation to meet Vermont’s energy and carbon-
reduction goals.  Exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 3. 
3. Under the Plan, the gas components of VGS’s rates will be adjusted by a Purchased 
Gas Adjustment (“PGA”), which remains largely unchanged from VGS’s most recent alternative 
regulation plan.  The PGA, which will adjust rates quarterly over the term of the Plan, will 
consist of an average cost per 100 cubic feet (“Ccf”) based on forecasted costs and volumes for 
the rate year and correct for any under- or over-collection of gas costs and weather normalization 
during the previous quarter.  McNeil pf. at 10; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 9-13. 
4. The non-gas components of VGS’s rates, which include VGS’s daily access and 
distribution charges (referred to as VGS’s base rates), will be set for the first year of the Plan 
through a traditional cost-of-service rate case.8  The Plan also includes a rate smoothing adjustor, 
which will reduce the base rates approved for 2024 and create a regulatory asset that will defer 
and amortize recovery of the reduced portion of the approved rates over the remaining term of 
the Plan.  The rate smoothing adjustor will aid in avoiding an immediate, significant rate increase 
caused by the termination of the System Expansion and Reliability Fund (“SERF”).  McNeil pf. 
at 9 and 19; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 3. 
 
8 See Petition of Vermont Gas Systems, Inc. for a change in rates and use of the System Expansion and 
Reliability Fund for an overall 0.1% increase in rates effective April 1, 2023, Case No. 23-0561-TF, an ongoing 
case that involves our review of a traditional cost-of-service rate filing from VGS.

Case No. 22-5085-PET 
 
Page 8 
 
 
5. The base rates for the remaining two years of the Plan will be based on: (1) 
adjustments to operating costs that will be pegged to fluctuations in inflationary indices, (2) a 
three-year rate base plan based on fixed capital spending limits, and (3) various pre-identified 
updates to non-operating costs.  McNeil pf. at 9; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 3. 
6. The Plan retains other ancillary components of VGS’s current alternative regulation 
plan, including performance, safety and service quality reporting consistent with VGS’s current 
Service Quality and Reliability Plan (“SQRP”), management of gas supply, dispute resolution, 
and the process for seeking amendments to the Plan.  McNeil pf. at 11. 
Operating Costs 
7. The Plan defines “operating costs” to include production, transmission, distribution, 
customer accounts, sales, administrative and general, and other income.  For the second and third 
years of the Plan, adjustments to VGS’s operating costs will be fixed to fluctuations in inflation 
indices.  McNeil pf. at 12-13; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 4. 
8. To more accurately reflect potential differences in inflation rates for labor expenses 
and goods and services, the Plan separates VGS’s operating costs into two categories.  The first 
category is intended to reflect the labor component of VGS’s operating costs.  It includes 69% of 
VGS’s overall operating costs and will be tied to fluctuations in the most recent 12-month 
percent change in the U.S. Bureau of Labor and Statistics Employment Cost Index.  The 
remaining 31% of VGS’s operating costs will be tied to the 12-month change in U.S. Bureau of 
Labor and Statistics Consumer Price Index for Northeast.  McNeil pf. at 12-13; exh. VGS-ALM-
4 at 4. 
9. The Plan also includes a firm 4% cap and a 2% floor for adjustments to VGS’s 
operating costs in years two and three.  Therefore, if inflation exceeds 4%, operating costs will 
only increase by 4%.  If the indices show inflation at less than 2%, operating costs will be 
adjusted by 2% for that year.  McNeil pf. at 12-13; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 4. 
Non-Operating Costs and Rate Base 
10. The Plan defines “non-operating costs” to include depreciation, taxes, and cost to 
finance rate base.  VGS’s total rate base for purposes of establishing non-operating costs during 
each year of the Plan will be based on a three-year rate base plan, which fixes VGS’s total plant

Case No. 22-5085-PET 
 
Page 9 
 
 
in service for the full three-year term of the Plan.  McNeil pf. at 13-14; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 4 
and Attachment 4. 
11. VGS’s rate base plan contemplates approximately $47.43 million of new capital 
investments over the term of the Plan.  Costs to finance rate base in each year of the Plan will be 
based on a debt-to-equity ratio of 50% to 50%.  McNeil pf. at 13-14; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 4 and 
Attachment 4. 
12. VGS will base depreciation expense on total plant in service as set forth in the rate 
base plan and the results of a depreciation study, which will be completed during the term of the 
Plan.  McNeil pf. at 13. 
13. VGS will update tax estimates based on the consumer price index for property tax, 
street fees, and other taxes.  Gross receipts and weatherization taxes will be based on forecasted 
revenue.  Income taxes will be based on VGS’s effective tax rate as applied to the cost to finance 
rate base and adjusted for amortization.  McNeil pf. at 13-14 
14. Adjustments to VGS’s non-operating costs during the term of the Plan can be made 
only for: (1) changes in short- or long-term debt rates as approved by the Commission in other 
cases, (2) changes to the authorized rate of return on equity investments (“ROE”) pursuant to the 
Plan, (3) adjustments to depreciation rates based on updates to the depreciation study, (4) 
Additional Innovation Capital approved by the Commission, and (5) updates to taxes.  McNeil 
pf. at 14. 
15. VGS’s ROE will initially be set as part of the Commission’s review of VGS’s base 
rate filing in Case No. 23-0561-TF, and then be formulaically adjusted for the remaining two 
years of the Plan based on fluctuations in the yield on 10-Year U.S. Treasury Notes.  McNeil pf. 
at 10; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 8.   
Earning Sharing and Exogenous Events 
16. The Plan includes an earning sharing mechanism (“ESM”) that will be based on a 
formula comparing VGS’s actual returns to its authorized rate of return for the prior fiscal year.  
The ESM includes symmetrical “dead-bands” that will result in no earning sharing if any over- 
or under-earnings are less than 50 basis points.  For over-earnings between 50 and 200 basis 
points, VGS will return 50% of the over-earnings to customers.  Conversely, for under-earnings

Case No. 22-5085-PET 
 
Page 10 
 
 
between 50 and 200 basis points, VGS absorbs 50% of the shortfall and recovers the other 50% 
from its customers.  McNeil pf. at 10; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 5-6. 
17. The Plan also includes an exogenous events mechanism that will allow VGS to 
recover costs for various events outside of VGS’s control.  This mechanism will cover events 
exceeding $200,000 in cost or benefit during a 12-month period.  It will apply to changes in state 
or federal tax law; unforeseen operational costs or capital investments; changes in Generally 
Accepted Accounting Principles; an ROE adjustment that exceeds 150 basis points; and other 
regulatory, judicial, or legislative changes affecting VGS, including rules or orders issued or 
promulgated by the Commission pursuant to the Affordable Heat Act.  McNeil pf. at 9; exh. 
VGS-ALM-4 at 6. 
Climate Action and Innovative Programs 
18. The Plan authorizes VGS to pursue new climate action and innovation programs.  It 
directs VGS to pursue and consider projects, programs, and services that support Vermont’s 
statewide energy goals by advancing promising technologies to facilitate efficient, lower carbon 
energy choices for Vermont customers, including, but not limited to: researching and seeking to 
pursue district energy; RNG and other alternative supply resources; uses of waste heat to lower 
usage of natural gas; power-to-gas projects; and more efficient or less carbon-intensive 
equipment for heating and industrial processes.  Morse pf. at 5-6; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 14-15. 
19. The Plan includes a $2 million annual budget for climate action and innovation 
spending, with $1.5 million anticipated to be directed at capital investments and $500,000 in 
expenses.  The Plan also includes provisions allowing VGS to seek permission from the 
Commission to increase its climate action and innovative spending budget over the term of the 
Plan.  McNeil pf. at 10; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 14. 
20. VGS proposes to include a provision in the Plan that would increase the monetary 
threshold for providing advance notice to the Commission and Department for new innovative 
service and climate action programs from $25,000, as in VGS’s current alternative regulation 
plan, to $100,000.  Morse pf. at 6; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 14.

Case No. 22-5085-PET 
 
Page 11 
 
 
21. VGS proposes that the Plan allow VGS to pursue Projects for “Vermont customers,” 
including entities that are not currently VGS customers.  Exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 14.9 
22. The Plan will include an alternative supply feature that will allow VGS to expand its 
renewable fuel options from RNG alone to include other forms of alternative supply, such as 
hydrogen or district heat.  The Plan also modifies the annual cap of 2% of new alternative supply 
to a three-year net 6% cap.  McNeil pf. at 10; Morse pf. at 5-6; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 12-13. 
23. VGS will assess the potential environmental benefits of new sources of alternative 
supply by comparing the supply source to the Vermont Climate Action plan’s established value 
of $128 per short ton (or $141 per metric ton) for the social cost of carbon on a portfolio-wide 
basis.  Morse pf. reb. at 7; exh. VGA-ALM-4 at 12; Tr. 6/19/23 at 33 (Morse), 55-57 (Jacobs), 
60-63 (Jacobs). 
24. The Plan includes performance reporting metrics that will allow the Commission and 
Department to review VGS’s performance in advancing state energy goals with its climate action 
initiatives and investments.  The metrics do not carry financial incentives or penalties, but they 
will provide insight into the effectiveness of various initiatives and technologies and aid in 
developing more cost-effective long-term strategies for VGS.  Jacobs pf. supp. at 3; McNeil pf. 
supp. at 22. 
B. 
Consistency With Section 218d Criteria 
Incentives to Provide Least-Cost Service 
[30 V.S.A. § 218d(a)(1)] 
25. The Plan will establish a system of regulation in which VGS has clear incentives to 
provide least-cost energy service to its customers.  This finding is supported by the additional 
findings below. 
26. The ESM establishes an incentive for VGS to provide least-cost service.  VGS will 
seek to minimize its costs and maximize its earnings to avoid sharing under-earnings with 
customers.  By operating efficiently, VGS can also generate over-earnings, which can be shared 
with customers.  Foley pf. supp. at 3. 
 
9 As discussed in more detail in our discussion section below, for purposes of establishing notice requirements 
for new climate action and innovation programs, VGS proposes that its service “footprint” be defined to include all 
locations within five miles of VGS’s nearest natural gas distribution line.  See Morse pf. reb. at 6.

Case No. 22-5085-PET 
 
Page 12 
 
 
27. Sharing of over- and under-earnings aligns VGS’s interests with its customers.  It 
encourages VGS to invest in necessary infrastructure while establishing an incentive for VGS to 
reduce costs and operate efficiently, as any over-earnings can be shared with customers.  This 
dynamic creates a situation where VGS has an opportunity to earn a fair return on its investments 
while providing affordable service to its customers.  Foley pf. supp. at 3. 
28. The alternative supply feature included in the PGA allows VGS to increase 
alternative supply as a percentage of its overall retail supply portfolio by 6% over the three-year 
term of the Plan, while also requiring VGS to consider environmental benefits compared to the 
Vermont Climate Action Plan’s established value of the social cost of carbon when considered in 
aggregate on a portfolio-wide basis.  Some resources included in the alternative supply feature 
may cost more, and other resources may cost less, but the cost of avoided carbon of the portfolio 
on an aggregate basis would be at or below the social cost of carbon.  Using the social cost of 
carbon as the metric to gauge cost-effectiveness of alternative fuel sources will ensure that 
VGS’s acquisition of these resources remains consistent with traditional least-cost planning 
principles.  Morse pf. reb. at 6-7; Tr. 6/19/23 at 83 (Jacobs); exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 12. 
Just and Reasonable Rates 
[30 V.S.A. § 218d(a)(2)] 
29. The Plan will allow VGS to provide just and reasonable rates for service to all classes 
of customers.  This finding is supported by the additional findings below. 
30. The first year of the Plan will include base rates that are determined to be just and 
reasonable through a traditional cost-of-service rate case.  Foley pf. supp. at 4; exh. VGS-ALM-4 
at 3. 
31. Subsequent adjustments to VGS’s base rates during the second and third years of the 
Plan will be limited to the rate of inflation and will be capped at no more than 4% per year.  
Foley pf. supp. at 4; McNeil pf. at 12; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 3. 
32. The Plan also includes a rate-smoothing adjustor, which will reduce “rate shock” and 
promote rate stability over the term of the Plan.  The rate-smoothing mechanism will help to 
provide a smooth rate trajectory by limiting an abrupt rate swing following the termination of the 
SERF.  Foley pf. supp. at 3; McNeil pf. at 19; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 3.

Case No. 22-5085-PET 
 
Page 13 
 
 
33. The PGA included in the Plan includes a quarterly weather normalization feature, 
which promotes stability for customers’ bills and protects against VGS generating windfalls and 
shortfalls caused by variable weather during the heating season.  McNeil pf. at 19-20; exh. VGS-
ALM-4 at 9. 
Safe and Reliable Service 
[30 V.S.A. § 218d(a)(3)] 
34. The Plan will allow VGS to deliver safe and reliable service.  This finding is 
supported by the additional findings below. 
35. The Plan incorporates compliance with VGS’s current SQRP.  Foley pf. supp. at 5; 
exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 15. 
36. The Plan includes an exogenous events recovery mechanism that will allow VGS to 
have swift recovery of costs associated with any unanticipated, high-cost events.  Foley pf. supp. 
at 5; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 6-7. 
State Energy Policy and Revenue Decoupling 
[30 V.S.A. § 218d(a)(4)] 
37. The Plan will offer incentives for innovations and improved performance that 
advance state energy policy such as increasing reliance on Vermont-based renewable energy and 
decreasing the extent to which the financial success of distribution utilities between rate cases is 
linked to increased sales to end-use customers and may be threatened by decreases in those sales.  
This finding is supported by the additional findings below. 
38. The Plan includes an annual $2 million budget for new climate action and innovation 
investments in programs and initiatives that will support Vermont’s statewide energy and 
greenhouse gas emission goals.  Jacobs pf. supp. at 3; exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 13-15. 
39. The Plan allows VGS to incrementally increase its supply of RNG and other 
alternative fuels.  When coupled with the requirement that emission reductions generated by 
these acquisitions be compared with the social cost of carbon, this feature of the Plan provides a 
mechanism for VGS to cost-effectively advance state energy policy.  Jacobs pf. supp. at 3; exh. 
VGS-ALM-4 at 13-15.

Case No. 22-5085-PET 
 
Page 14 
 
 
40. The reporting metrics included in the Plan will enable the Commission and 
Department to review VGS’s performance in advancing state energy goals.  Jacobs pf. supp. at 3; 
exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 15.  
41. Implementation of VGS’s climate action plan will likely result in decreased sales of 
traditional natural gas.  In the near term, the Plan will allow VGS to invest in innovation and 
climate action while also tracking performance so that VGS can further develop sustainable 
long-term strategies.  McNeil pf. at 22. 
42. The inclusion of the PGA and the ESM in the Plan will decouple the link between 
VGS’s financial performance and sales to end-use customers.  McNeil pf. at 16-17; Foley pf. 
supp. at 3. 
43. The Plan can also be modified to ensure that VGS is able to comply with any 
requirements that may be developed under the Affordable Heat Act.  Morse pf. reb. at 9; exh. 
VGS-ALM-4 at 15. 
Service Quality, Reliability, and Service Choices 
[30 V.S.A. § 218d(a)(5)] 
44. The Plan will improve the quality of VGS’s service, reliability, and service choices.  
This finding is supported by the additional findings below. 
45. The Plan maintains VGS’s existing SQRP.  Jacobs pf. supp. at 3; exh. VGS-ALM-4 
at 15. 
46. The Plan will continue VGS’s implementation of RNG into its supply stream.  It will 
also enable investment into innovative programs, including electrification offerings through 
technologies such as heat pump water heaters and hybrid heating systems.  These investments 
and technologies will provide VGS customers with new service choices over the term of the 
Plan.  Jacobs pf. supp. at 3. 
Innovation in the Provision of Service 
[30 V.S.A. § 218d(a)(6)] 
47. The Plan will encourage innovation in the provision of service.  This finding is 
supported by the additional findings below.

Case No. 22-5085-PET 
 
Page 15 
 
 
48. The Plan continues VGS’s climate action and innovation programs, which include a 
budget for new investments in initiatives to support Vermont’s clean energy goals through 
activities that promote emission reductions.  Jacobs pf. supp. at 4. 
49. The Plan enables VGS to provide services beyond its traditional natural gas utility 
platform and attempt to reduce carbon emissions through emerging technologies, service 
offerings, and renewable supply.  McNeil pf. at 23. 
Balanced Risks and Rewards 
[30 V.S.A. § 218d(a)(7)] 
50. The Plan establishes a reasonably balanced system of risks and rewards that 
encourages VGS to operate as efficiently as possible using sound management practices.  This 
finding is supported by the additional findings below. 
51. The initial ROE for the Plan will be set as part of a traditional cost-of-service rate 
case.  Consistent with VGS’s current alternative regulation plan, future adjustments to the ROE 
during the term of the Plan will be calculated as one-half the change in the composite 10-Year 
Treasury Note Rate for each date between March and June as compared to the same time period 
during the following year.  Foley pf. supp. at 5, exh. VGS-ALM-4 at 8. 
52. The Plan includes the ESM, which ensures that savings, if any, are shared with 
customers.  McNeil pf. at 23.

VII. 
DISCUSSION 
A. Introduction 
 
Having reviewed VGS’s proposed Plan, the evidentiary record developed throughout this 
case, and the parties’ legal arguments, we conclude that the Plan, subject to the modifications 
described below, satisfies the statutory criteria set out in 30 V.S.A. § 218d and will promote the 
public good.  Therefore, we approve the Plan subject to those modifications. 
 
The proposed Plan carries forward many components of VGS’s existing alternative 
regulation plan, including the PGA and the climate action and innovation programs.  We agree 
with the parties that these components of the Plan have benefitted VGS and its ratepayers alike in 
furtherance of the statutory objectives set out in Section 218d.  The Plan builds on the foundation 
of VGS’s prior alternative regulation plans with the addition of the rate base plan, which is 
grounded in a fixed capital expenditure budget, and by fixing VGS’s operating costs to inflation 
with a firm 4% cap.  These components of the Plan will enhance transparency into VGS’s 
underlying rate drivers and will benefit ratepayers with increased rate stability.  These benefits 
are particularly important in light of the recent volatility in natural gas markets and high 
inflationary pressures throughout the broader economy. 
 
The Plan also affords VGS greater flexibility to pursue necessary changes to its business 
practices.  It establishes firm capital budgets for pursuing new technologies and services that will 
ideally reduce VGS’s overall carbon footprint without shifting excessive costs onto its 
ratepayers, many of whom will need to continue to rely on VGS’s services for the foreseeable 
future.  It also enables VGS to make targeted expansions to its portfolio of alternative fuel 
sources, which allows for cost-effective reductions to VGS’s carbon emissions from the fuel it 
supplies to customers.   
 
We recognize that VGS will need to substantially overhaul its traditional business 
services and aggressively pursue new programs and technologies to comply with Vermont’s

Affordable Heat Act and which may be enacted by the Legislature.  At the same time, VGS will

B. 
Disputed Issues 
VGS Option to Seek an Extension of the Plan 
 
We agree with the Department that the option to extend the Plan should be limited to one 
year.  As the Department notes, the Plan is designed to coincide with the three-year term of the 
rate-smoothing mechanism.  The Plan also includes fixed rate-base adjustments that are designed 
around a three-year forecast for VGS’s capital expenditures.  Based on these factors, we are 
concerned about pushing back the timeframe for when VGS will next need to reset rates through 
a traditional cost-of-service review.  Stated differently, we do not want VGS’s rates to become 
significantly divorced from its actual cost-of-service, which could result in an abrupt rate shift in 
a future rate case.  However, as the Department recognizes, the timing for the potential 
implementation of the initial requirements of the Affordable Heat Act may coincide with the 
expiration of the Plan.  We agree that this potential coincidence could result in administrative 
inefficiencies because of the possibility for significant changes to the statutory and regulatory 
landscape for the thermal heating sector.  Therefore, we agree with the Department that the Plan 
should include an extension option, but that option should be limited to one year. 
 
We also stress that this component of the Plan only allows VGS the option to seek our 
approval of a one-year extension of the Plan.  To the extent there are unforeseen circumstances 
that would justify a longer extension, VGS can still seek our permission to have the Plan 
amended to allow for additional extensions of the Plan.  Indeed, Paragraph 12 of the Plan states 
that VGS or the Department may “request that this Plan be amended to modify its existing

recommendation, VGS is not foreclosed from seeking additional extensions of the plan in the 
future.  We also note that the inclusion of an option to request a one-year extension of the Plan 
does not guarantee our future approval of that request. 
Monetary Threshold for Reporting New Climate Action Projects 
 
We decline to adopt either of the parties’ positions on issues related to advance notice for 
new climate action and innovative projects.  Instead, we direct that VGS modify the Plan to 
preserve the existing $25,000 reporting threshold for all new climate action and innovative 
projects.  We recognize that the Department agrees with VGS’s proposal to increase this 
threshold to $100,000 for projects that will be pursued within VGS’s existing service territory for 
the benefit of VGS customers.  However, we are concerned that increasing the reporting 
threshold to $100,000 will greatly diminish transparency into and regulatory oversight over 
VGS’s spending on innovative projects.  These projects often involve nascent technologies and 
investments in products and services that may entail relatively high financial or performance risk 
for VGS and its ratepayers.  Although we agree that VGS should be allowed to have increased 
flexibility to pursue non-traditional projects and services that reduce carbon emissions, it remains 
important for the Commission and Department to maintain close regulatory oversight of these 
projects and services to ensure they include adequate safeguards and ratepayer protections.  We 
also remain concerned about VGS’s ability to use its position as a monopoly service provider to 
gain an unfair advantage in competitive marketplaces. 
 
This decision should not result in significant regulatory burdens on VGS.  As VGS notes 
in its testimony, the company has been required to file advance notices for only seven new 
climate action and innovation projects during the term of its existing alternative regulation 
plan.27  Although there may be an increase in the number of these projects over the term of the 
Plan, we are not convinced that VGS faces significant burdens in presenting this information to 
its regulators.  Additionally, establishing a firm reporting threshold for all projects eliminates any 
ambiguities as to which projects fall within VGS’s “footprint” and provides VGS with certainty

Social Cost of Carbon 
 
VGS agrees to the Department’s recommendation to use a value of $128 per short ton, or 
$141 per metric ton, for the social cost of carbon as the metric for evaluating the cost-
effectiveness of new acquisitions of alternative supply resources on a portfolio-wide basis during 
the term of the Plan.  This value reflects the Vermont Climate Council’s calculation of the social 
cost of carbon using a 2% discount rate, which was included in the Climate Council’s 2021 
Climate Action Plan. 
 
Having reviewed the parties’ testimony on this issue, including the various witnesses’ 
testimony during the evidentiary hearing, we agree with the Department’s recommendation to 
include the social cost of carbon metric in the Plan as agreed to by the parties.  We recognize that 
the Vermont Climate Council may update the underlying calculation for the social cost of carbon 
in future iterations of the Climate Action Plan.  It is also possible that the development of 
enforceable mandates under the Affordable Heat Act or other future legislative or regulatory 
mandates may render this metric unnecessary or moot for VGS with respect to its carbon 
reduction obligations.  However, for the immediate future, which includes the three-year term 
covered by the Plan, the social cost of carbon metric establishes an objective benchmark for 
assessing the cost-effectiveness of VGS’s acquisition decisions as it pursues new sources of 
alternative fuels.  Accordingly, we conclude that it is appropriate for this metric to be included in 
the Plan.
